threats.title: The same authorization is settled twice
threats.threat: A seller, a buyer or anyone holding a payment sends the same PAYMENT-SIGNATURE to /settle again, one after another or many at once, hoping the payer is charged more than once.
threats.stellar: An exact or upto authorization is a Soroban authorization entry whose nonce the host consumes when the entry is used; a second use fails on chain with Error(Auth, ExistingValue). The nonce lives under the payer's own address, for G and C accounts alike, until the signature expires. A duplicate that reaches the network is included and fails, so the sponsor still pays its fee.
threats.preconditions: A copy of a payment payload that was already sent to /settle.
threats.impact: Without protection: one wasted sponsor fee per duplicate. The payer can never be charged twice, because the host refuses the second use of the nonce.

mitigations.text: One settlement record per (network, payer, nonce), claimed before any RPC work; later requests answer from the record instead of submitting.
The settle path looks the authorization up first and answers a repeat with the recorded response, marked as a repeat.
A request whose terms differ from the recorded request is refused, never given the stored success.
Verify reads the ledger and refuses an authorization that is being settled or already was.

threats.title: The same authorization in a new envelope
threats.threat: An attacker wraps an already settled authorization entry in a transaction of different bytes (another source, sequence or fee) so it is not recognised as a repeat.
threats.stellar: The authorization is bound to its invocation, not to the transaction, so it can be placed in any envelope. The host refuses the consumed nonce at apply time; a facilitator that only compared envelope bytes would submit it and pay the fee.
threats.preconditions: A copy of a settled authorization entry.
threats.impact: One wasted sponsor fee per attempt if it reached the network.

mitigations.text: The settlement key is the payer's address and nonce, read from the authorization entry, not the envelope hash.
A different envelope for a recorded authorization is refused with the idempotency conflict, naming the recorded transaction.

threats.residual: None: nothing is submitted.

threats.title: An authorization replayed on another network
threats.threat: A payment signed for stellar:testnet is presented for stellar:pubnet, or the reverse.
threats.stellar: The signed preimage (HashIdPreimageSorobanAuthorization) includes the network id, the SHA-256 of the network passphrase, so a signature is only valid on the network it was made for.
threats.preconditions: A signed payment for one network.
threats.impact: None on chain: signature verification fails on the other network.

mitigations.text: The network id is part of every signed preimage the buyer's guard decodes and checks.
A request is served only on the network its requirements name, and a payload for another network is refused.

threats.title: Paid once, served many times
threats.threat: A buyer pays once and sends the same PAYMENT-SIGNATURE several times, concurrently or later. A stock upfront seller calls /settle without /verify and serves on success, and an idempotent facilitator answers every repeat with the same success.
threats.stellar: Nothing Stellar-specific allows it: it follows from answering repeats with the stored result, which the x402 idempotency requirement asks for. The Stellar part is that the answer carries the one settlement transaction hash, which a seller can deduplicate on.
threats.preconditions: A seller that serves on a successful /settle without remembering which settlements it already served.
threats.impact: The seller serves a paid resource more than once for one payment. The buyer is charged once.

mitigations.text: Every repeated /settle answer carries a repeat marker in EXTENSION-RESPONSES (rail402.settlement.repeat).
The seller helpers refuse a second request whose settlement is a repeat or a transaction already served.
In the authorization flow, verify refuses an authorization that is being settled or was.

threats.title: An upto authorization settled for zero stays usable
threats.threat: A seller settles an upto payment for zero, then tries to charge the same authorization again for a positive amount.
threats.stellar: An on-chain zero settlement still uses the payer's authorization entry, so the host consumes its nonce like any other settlement. An off-chain zero (UPTO_ZERO_SETTLEMENT=offchain) sends nothing, so the nonce stays unused on chain until the signature expires.
threats.preconditions: An upto payment settled for zero.
threats.impact: Without protection, a second settlement of the same authorization for up to the cap.

mitigations.text: The upto contract consumes the payer's nonce for a zero settlement too.

An off-chain zero is a terminal record in the settlement ledger, so a later request for any amount is answered from it or refused as a conflict; only the named authority can settle on chain, and it is Rail402's.

threats.residual: With off-chain zeros and STORE=memory, a restart forgets the record; the authorization then stays settleable by Rail402's own authority until it expires. Use Postgres wherever off-chain zeros are enabled.

threats.title: A copied exact authorization lands first
threats.threat: Someone who sees the settlement envelope (the seller, an RPC operator, a validator's pending queue) copies the payer's authorization entry into a transaction of their own and gets it included before Rail402's.
threats.stellar: A Soroban authorization is a bearer instrument for exactly one invocation: whoever submits it can only make the signed transfer happen, from the payer to payTo for the signed amount. It cannot be redirected. Rail402's own transaction then fails on the consumed nonce and its fee is spent.
threats.preconditions: Access to the envelope between signing and inclusion, and an account to pay the copy's fee.
threats.impact: One wasted sponsor fee per event. The attacker pays its own fee and gains nothing; the payment settles as signed.

mitigations.text: Rail402 submits as soon as the settle-time simulation passes, which leaves little time to copy the entry.
Signed envelopes and authorizations are redacted from logs.
Wasted fees are counted, so griefing is visible and bounded by the hourly budget.

threats.residual: The wasted fee is not recoverable. Each event costs the attacker its own fee too.

threats.title: The seller is told the payment failed although it settled
threats.threat: After a front-run, Rail402's transaction fails with a consumed nonce and the seller is told the payment failed, although the payer was charged.
threats.stellar: The chain holds the proof: the nonce entry's last-modified ledger, and in that ledger a successful transaction whose address credential (payer, nonce, signature expiration) and root invocation are byte-equal to the payer's signed entry, with the matching token transfer event.
threats.preconditions: A front-run as in F1.
threats.impact: Without reconciliation the seller withholds a resource that was paid for.

mitigations.text: A failed settlement whose nonce was consumed is reconciled: Rail402 finds the other transaction on chain, proves it carried the same signed invocation after the request was claimed, and answers success with its hash.
Proof requires a byte-equal root invocation and credential; a different invocation for the same nonce stays a failure.

threats.residual: A public RPC keeps only a window of ledgers; a settlement reconciled after that window stays failed. Reconciliation runs immediately after the failure, well inside the window.

threats.title: A third party settles an upto payment for another amount by submitting it
threats.threat: Someone holding an upto payload (the buyer, the seller, a TLS-terminating proxy, a log, an RPC operator who sees the settlement envelope) submits it themselves for another amount up to the cap, such as zero or the whole cap, before or instead of the seller's settlement.
threats.stellar: The payer's signature covers the cap, not the amount. The upto contract therefore also requires the authorization of the settlement authority named in the signed terms, and Rail402 makes that authority the operation's source account, so its authorization is the transaction's own signature and cannot be copied into another transaction.
threats.preconditions: A copy of an upto payload.
threats.impact: None: the network refuses a settlement that the settlement authority did not authorize, and Rail402's settlement proceeds. The same request through the facilitator's own /settle is F5.

mitigations.text: The contract requires terms.facilitator to authorize settle(payer, terms, amount), so the authority's authorization covers one amount and nothing else.
Rail402 signs as the authority through a source-account credential that exists only inside its own transaction.

threats.title: Another holder of the authority settles first
threats.threat: Two replicas sharing the sponsor secret, or a stale process, settle the same upto payment; one lands first with a different amount than the seller asked for.
threats.stellar: Only a transaction signed by the authority can land; the landed amount is readable from the settle arguments and the upto_settled event.
threats.preconditions: Two processes that hold the same authority key.
threats.impact: Without reconciliation the seller gets a false failure, or a success for an amount it did not request.

mitigations.text: The later settlement is answered with the landed transaction when it settled the same amount, and with settle_upto_stellar_settled_elsewhere, naming both amounts, when it did not.

threats.residual: None beyond one wasted fee.

threats.title: A payload holder fixes the upto amount through the facilitator's /settle
threats.threat: Someone holding an upto payload asks the facilitator's own /settle to settle it for another amount up to the cap, such as zero or the whole cap, before the seller does.
threats.stellar: The payer's signature covers the cap, not the amount, and the facilitator is the settlement authority: whichever accepted /settle request comes first decides the amount it authorizes, and the payer's nonce then makes the authorization single-use.
threats.preconditions: A copy of an upto payload and access to the facilitator's /settle (keyless on the public testnet service).
threats.impact: The first accepted request fixes the amount anywhere in [0, cap] to payTo: a buyer who settles zero first leaves the seller unpaid for that request, and anyone who settles the cap first charges the buyer the full cap. The seller's own later request for a different amount is refused as an idempotency conflict. Funds never go elsewhere and never exceed the cap.

mitigations.text: The facilitator settles an authorization once: the first accepted amount wins, and a later request for a different amount is refused with settle_upto_stellar_idempotency_conflict naming the amount that holds it.

Operators can require API keys for /verify and /settle per network, so only known sellers can settle; the payload travels only from buyer to seller over TLS, and sellers settle before releasing a buffered response.

threats.residual: Accepted for payload holders on a keyless facilitator: a buyer or anyone who sees the payload can fix the amount through /settle before the seller (unpaid seller compute and one sponsor fee, or the buyer charged up to its own cap). Operators who need more require API keys for /settle.

threats.title: A payment passes simulation and fails at apply
threats.threat: A payer spends the balance, or changes a smart account's state, after the settle-time simulation and before inclusion, so the settlement is included and fails.
threats.stellar: Soroban resource fees are charged when a transaction is included, success or failure; the sponsor pays through the fee bump. Simulation runs against the latest ledger, so a change made in the ledgers between simulation and inclusion is not seen.
threats.preconditions: A payer (or its smart-account policy) able to act within about one ledger of the settlement.
threats.impact: One wasted sponsor fee per event, never more than the fee ceiling. No funds move.

mitigations.text: Settle simulates again with the current ledger, so a change made before settle is refused without submitting.
The failure is named from the transaction's diagnostic events and counted as wasted fee.
The hourly fee budget and the reserve floor bound the total a griefer can burn.

threats.residual: The race inside one ledger cannot be closed by a facilitator that does not hold the funds. Each event costs the payer an on-chain transaction of its own.

threats.title: An authorization expires between submission and inclusion
threats.threat: A payment is settled with an authorization whose expiration ledger passes while the transaction waits for inclusion.
threats.stellar: Validity runs through signatureExpirationLedger inclusive; the transaction's time bound can outlive it. An included transaction whose authorization expired fails and its fee is spent.
threats.preconditions: A payment settled at the very end of its validity window.
threats.impact: One wasted sponsor fee.

mitigations.text: Settle refuses an authorization that expires within a one-ledger margin of the current ledger.
An upto settlement's ledger bounds end at the expiration ledger, so the network refuses it before inclusion and no fee is spent.

threats.residual: For exact, a transaction that waits longer than the margin in the network's queue can still fail this way; it is named and counted as wasted.

threats.title: A payment that is expensive to settle
threats.threat: A payer submits a payment whose settlement needs large resources: a heavy __check_auth, a token that writes a lot of state, or rent for entries it extends.
threats.stellar: Soroban fees depend on the instructions, ledger reads and writes, and rent of the invocation, which the payer's account and the token contract choose. The fee is known from simulation before anything is signed.
threats.preconditions: A smart account or token contract whose calls are costly.
threats.impact: Without a ceiling, an arbitrary fee per settlement.

mitigations.text: Verify and settle refuse a payment whose simulated fee exceeds MAX_TX_FEE_STROOPS (UPTO_MAX_TX_FEE_STROOPS for upto), before signing.
The inclusion-fee bid is capped.

threats.residual: A payment just under the ceiling costs up to the ceiling. Operators accepting tokens that pay rent on read raise the ceiling knowingly (the TEST6 token needs about 1,000,000 stroops on testnet).

threats.title: A flood of valid small payments
threats.threat: Someone makes many real, valid payments of the smallest amount to drain the sponsor through fees.
threats.stellar: Every valid settlement costs the sponsor a fee of tens of thousands of stroops, far more than a one-unit USDC payment is worth.
threats.preconditions: Funds for many small payments.
threats.impact: Sponsor XLM spent at the attacker's pace.

mitigations.text: An hourly fee budget, shared by replicas through the settlement ledger, stops new settlements once reached; pubnet refuses to start without one.
Per-client rate limits and API keys on /verify and /settle; API keys must be decided explicitly for pubnet.
Per-asset minimum amounts for exact payments and upto caps (an upto settlement may still be zero; see U6).

A client with many addresses passes the rate limit, so the budget is the real bound: once it is spent, every settlement is refused until the hour moves on, which trades availability for the sponsor's balance. On pubnet the budget is required, and pricing, keys and minimums are an operator decision.

threats.title: The sponsor falls below its reserve
threats.threat: The sponsor's balance runs low, from normal use or an attack, until fee bumps start failing mid-settlement.
threats.stellar: The sponsor also carries the base reserves of the channel accounts and the upto authority, which it sponsors; below them it cannot pay fees at all.
threats.preconditions: Sustained settlement volume or an attack as in S4.
threats.impact: Settlements fail after signing; the service becomes unavailable.

mitigations.text: Settlements are refused below SPONSOR_RESERVE_XLM before any RPC work, with a retryable code.
/ready fails below MIN_SPONSOR_BALANCE_XLM and /health reports it.

threats.title: Duplicate submissions of one settlement
threats.threat: Retries, concurrent requests or two replicas submit the same settlement more than once.
threats.stellar: Each submitted transaction consumes a channel sequence number and pays its own fee; the second one fails on the consumed nonce.
threats.preconditions: Concurrent or repeated requests for one payment.
threats.impact: Wasted fees and sequence conflicts.

mitigations.text: One claim per authorization across replicas; only the claim holder signs and submits.
A crashed settlement is resumed from its recorded envelope bytes, never rebuilt.

threats.title: Restoring archived state inside a buyer's payment
threats.threat: A settlement touches an archived contract instance or entry, and the transaction would restore it, billing the restoration rent to the sponsor as part of the payment.
threats.stellar: Since protocol 23 a freshly simulated invocation of an archived persistent entry restores it automatically inside the transaction, and the fee payer pays the rent.
threats.preconditions: An archived settlement contract, token instance or balance entry.
threats.impact: Rent paid by the sponsor on behalf of whoever let the entry expire.

mitigations.text: A simulation that reports archived state is refused: the upto settlement contract with invalid_upto_stellar_settlement_contract_archived, other entries with the archived-state code; nothing is submitted.
Exact payments name archived state from the simulation's restore preamble.

threats.title: Forged listing metadata or price
threats.threat: A buyer (or a seller's buggy client) echoes a resource block with a false description, price or schema in the payment, hoping the catalog publishes it.
threats.stellar: Nothing on chain describes the resource; the settlement proves only that a payment to payTo happened. The metadata must be confirmed at its origin.
threats.preconditions: One real settlement to the seller.
threats.impact: Misleading listings shown to buyers and agents.

mitigations.text: An HTTP resource, or an MCP tool at an http(s) endpoint, is published only after its own 402 (for a tool, the answer to an unpaid tools/call over MCP) confirms payTo, price and metadata; what is published always comes from that answer, so echoed metadata never changes a listing on its own.
MCP tools are asked through safe-fetch with the MCP client: the tool must be declared in tools/list and its unpaid call must answer with the x402 PaymentRequired.

threats.title: Taking over another seller's listing
threats.threat: An attacker pays a URL that belongs to another seller, but to its own payTo, to take over or modify that listing.
threats.stellar: The settled payTo is the only identity the facilitator has proven, from a settlement that moved value to it. An upto zero moves nothing and proves nothing, so it never catalogs.
threats.preconditions: A settlement for the victim's URL to the attacker's account.
threats.impact: Payments for a listed resource redirected to the attacker.

mitigations.text: A listing is bound to the settled payTo; another payTo is refused with bazaar_owner_conflict, and ownership moves only when the origin names the new payTo.

A settlement that moved nothing (an upto zero, on-chain or off) never catalogs. A settlement that moved one base unit does not help either: a listing is published only with what its own origin answers (P1, P9).

threats.title: Hostile JSON Schema in listing metadata
threats.threat: Metadata carries a schema with a catastrophic regular expression, a combinatorial check, deep nesting or an external $ref.
threats.stellar: None: this is a property of the catalog, which validates schemas it receives in payments.
threats.preconditions: One settlement carrying the schema.
threats.impact: Catalog workers stalled, or the service fetching arbitrary URLs.

mitigations.text: Schemas compile and validate in a worker with a time budget and a bounded queue; external references are refused.

threats.title: A tampered payment or a false settlement report
threats.threat: A scheme client changes the payload after the guard approved it, or a seller reports a settlement that did not happen, reports another payment's transaction hash, or settles through its own contract so the transaction does not look like a direct settlement.
threats.stellar: The host records every authorization nonce it consumes in a temporary ledger entry keyed by the payer and the nonce, and only the entry the payer signed can consume it. A transaction used a payment's authorization exactly when it carries the payer's entry with that payment's nonce and its meta creates that nonce entry, whatever its call path: Soroban matches an entry below the top-level call, so a wrapper, router or batch contract can settle it too, and one transaction can consume several nonces. A transfer event alone says nothing about which authorization moved the money.
threats.preconditions: A malicious scheme client or seller.
threats.impact: Paying for something else, believing a payment failed or succeeded wrongly, or a session budget that under-counts what moved.

mitigations.text: The guard compares the payload with what it signed.

A payment is proven only by its own nonce: a transaction that consumed it settles the reservation whatever its shape, for the exact price, or for upto the amount the signed settlement contract recorded for the signed terms (the whole cap when that cannot be read). A consumed authorization is never released.

A reported hash is only a claim against the payment it was reported for and counts as spent; it never removes a transaction from another payment's proof. Budget returns only when the authorization has expired and no transaction in its validity range consumed it.
An expired payment the RPC can no longer prove either way counts as spent at its whole amount and is no longer reconciled.

threats.title: The relay used to reach private networks or as an open proxy
threats.threat: A visitor, or a script calling the Playground's API, asks the relay to fetch a loopback, private or cloud-metadata address, a name that resolves to one, or a seller that redirects to one; or uses the relay to send volume to third parties from the Playground's address.
threats.stellar: Nothing Stellar-specific: the relay exists because Rail402 and most x402 sellers answer no CORS headers, so a page cannot call them itself. A paid request through it carries a PAYMENT-SIGNATURE the visitor's own key made.
threats.preconditions: Network access to the Playground server.
threats.impact: Without protection: requests into the server's network, or the Playground's address used for abuse.

mitigations.text: The relay sends with safe-fetch under a fixed policy: https on port 443 to public addresses only, DNS answers checked and pinned, redirects refused except same-origin hops for unpaid probes, request and answer size limits.
By host name, it never contacts the Playground itself (its public host and the platform's generated domain), the facilitator, the Bazaar or an operator-denied host.
Per-client, global, per-host, in-flight and daily byte limits, with Retry-After, and a switch to turn the relay off.

Global limits are fair-shared: one network (an IPv4 address or an IPv6 /48) holds at most an eighth of a pool, or its per-client limit when that is larger; clients are keyed by IPv4 address or IPv6 /56.

Only a payment that decodes as an x402 payment counts against the paid limits, whether it travels in PAYMENT-SIGNATURE or in an MCP tool call's _meta; anything else is refused before a token is taken.

The demo seller has a paid pool of its own, a paid request that reached no seller gives the shared pool its token back, and the lab sellers return it when the facilitator was never asked, so payments that only have the right shape cannot use up the pools the demo flows need.

Unpaid requests wait no longer than the SDK's probe timeouts; bodies pass only as JSON, text or octet-stream; slots of an abandoned upload or an unread answer are released; connections to hosts other than the demo seller are closed after each answer.
Unpaid requests and answer bytes are also limited per network, bytes for all clients per day, requests in flight per destination host, and each network gets at most its share of a host's budget.

threats.residual: For a client that is not a browser, the relay is an open https egress to public hosts at the Playground's address, bounded only by the limits; IP-keyed limits cannot stop a client with many addresses or networks. The payment check stops only malformed payments: a payment that merely has the right shape is counted as paid, so enough addresses can still use up a shared paid pool for a minute at a time. Loop and deny lists match host names: another name of a denied host is caught only when the operator lists it. Its user agent names the Playground, and the operator can deny hosts or switch the relay off.

threats.title: Another site drives the relay from a visitor's browser
threats.threat: A page on another origin makes a visitor's browser send requests through the Playground's relay, seller check or proxies, or reads their answers.
threats.stellar: The relay holds no key and no session, so a forged request carries no authority the attacker lacks; a payment needs a signature from the key in the Playground's own page.
threats.preconditions: A visitor with the Playground open, or not, visits the attacker's page.
threats.impact: Without protection: the Playground's relay used through visitors' browsers.

mitigations.text: The relay needs its own request headers, which a cross-site form cannot set; a browser's Sec-Fetch-Site must be same-origin and its Origin the Playground's public origin.
The relay answers no CORS headers, so no other origin can read an answer.
The Bazaar and /supported proxies refuse another site's requests the same way, so no page can spend their shared upstream budget through visitors' browsers.

threats.title: Script injected into the page uses the testnet key
threats.threat: Seller-supplied text (a description, an error, a response body) or a third-party script runs in the page and signs with, or reads, the wallet's key.
threats.stellar: The key signs Soroban authorization entries through the SDK's signing guard; a script in the page could ask it to sign within the visitor's caps.
threats.preconditions: A seller or listing the visitor's page displays.
threats.impact: Without protection: testnet funds spent within the caps, or the testnet key read out.

mitigations.text: A content security policy without inline or third-party script, styles or frames from the Playground's origin only, and connections only to the configured Stellar endpoints.
Seller text is rendered as text, and an untrusted URL becomes a link only when it is https and parses; no view renders raw markup.
The stored seed is encrypted under a key WebCrypto generated as non-extractable; only the wallet modules touch the key.

The CSP and the absence of markup sinks make that unlikely. The key is meant for testnet only, and the import field says never to paste a key that holds real funds.

threats.title: The seller check used to scan ports or private hosts
threats.threat: A visitor submits private addresses, other ports or many URLs to the seller check to map the server's network or to load third parties.
threats.stellar: The check runs the SDK's seller checks: the URL's 402, its discovery metadata, whether payTo can receive the asset, and the seller's stellar.toml and home domain.
threats.preconditions: Network access to the Playground server.
threats.impact: Without protection: a port scanner inside the server's network.

mitigations.text: The check fetches with https on port 443 to public addresses only, through the Playground's own facilitator, in the hosted configuration.
Ten checks per minute per client and sixty for all clients, and a switch to turn it off.

threats.title: The lab sellers take real payments or pollute the catalog
threats.threat: The Playground's misbehaving sellers (the offers, the greedy upto route) take a payment that sticks, or every visitor's sandbox sale adds a listing to the public Bazaar.
threats.stellar: An upto authorization caps what any settlement can move; Rail402 refuses a settlement above it, and the settlement contract enforces the cap on chain too.
threats.preconditions: A visitor running the lab.
threats.impact: Without protection: visitors charged more than they authorized, or a catalog flooded with sample listings.

mitigations.text: The offers answer a 402 only and never verify or settle.
The greedy route asks to settle twice its cap, which Rail402's upto rules refuse; it declares no discovery metadata.
The sandbox route answers the same 402 for every city and visitor, so it is one listing paid to one operator account.
Its discovery metadata always carries the declared example city, never the one a request names, and a path that is not a city name gets no 402, so no payer writes text into the shared listing.

threats.title: The stored wallet read or overspent
threats.threat: The wallet's stored record is swapped or tampered with, or two tabs spend one session budget at the same time.
threats.stellar: The budget ledger reserves each payment before it is signed; two writers of one stored ledger could each see room the other already used.
threats.preconditions: Access to the browser profile, or two open tabs.
threats.impact: Without protection: a different key loaded, or the session budget exceeded.

mitigations.text: The stored record is bound to its address and network; a tampered or rebound record is refused.
One tab holds the wallet through a Web Lock; the others are read-only.
A stored ledger that cannot be read is refused until it is reset, never silently emptied.

threats.title: Payments or the key leak into logs, traces or storage
threats.threat: A PAYMENT-SIGNATURE, a signed authorization or the key ends up in the server's logs or traces, an error, the page's storage, a run report or a request to a third party.
threats.stellar: A signed authorization is spendable by whoever holds it until it expires.
threats.preconditions: Any run.
threats.impact: Without protection: an authorization replayable by whoever reads the channel, or the key exposed.

mitigations.text: The relay logs the host, status and outcome only, never the target path, query, headers or body.
The lab sellers' trace header carries verify and settle outcomes, never payloads.
Run reports are built from the run's events, which hold no key, signature, preimage or payment header.
